messages:
Sam: Quick nsys question — trying to capture short KV-cache eviction kernels (~150-400us) that happen during batching. Full 60s captures blow up to tens of GB. How do people tune nsys to catch these tiny hotspots without huge traces?

Jess: Short answer: do many targeted short captures + NVTX bracketing. For KV evictions you want to capture the exact region where eviction happens (capture-range=nvtx) and use shorter duration. Also filter to the PID or binary to avoid noise. :mag:

Lee: FWIW here's a command we use as a template:

```
nsys profile --output=kv-evict-1 \
  --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt \
  --capture-range=nvtx \
  --capture-range-start=nvtxTagStart \
  --capture-range-end=nvtxTagEnd \
  --sample=cpu:200us \
  --duration=3s \
  --force-overwrite --sample-one-file \
  --target-process-name=my_server_binary
```

Lee: Notes: 1) we bracket eviction with NVTX push/pop in the runtime (NVTX tags around the eviction routine). 2) multiple 3s runs are cheaper than one long run. 3) use the target process filter so system noise (other tenants, docker shim) is excluded.

Sam: Nice. Do we ever rely on the OSRT trace only (no cuda) for these short kernels? The kernels are tiny but show up in CUDA timeline as many tiny launches.

Jess: For kernel timeline and launch overhead you want cuda + osrt. cuda shows kernel execution; osrt helps with driver/submit/launch timing. nvtx gives the semantic context. Putting all three is helpful but increases size. If disk is the limit, try toggling osrt off and do a second focused run with osrt on when you need launch timing.

Sam: Got it. Any tips on sample/interval? I used --sample=cpu previously with default and barely saw anything.

Lee: We set sample to cpu:100us or cpu:200us for dense short-kernel workloads. If you lower to 50us you get much bigger files. Also, prefer multiple short samples instead of one long. Another trick: use --trace-level=low (if available) to reduce event verbosity.

perf-bot: Tip: if you're seeing huge .nsys-rep files, run `nsys stats` to inspect timeline sizes and then `nsys export` to slice out ranges.

Jess: Also consider enabling `--trace-fork-before-exec=false` or similar flags to avoid tracing child processes you don't care about (platform-specific). And run with `--output` to a fast NVMe temp directory, then compress or move.

Sam: We do NVTX already. Here's the tiny NVTX snippet we add in runtime around eviction: 

```cpp
nvtxRangePushA("kv:evict:start");
// eviction work
nvtxRangePop();
```

Sam: After doing a few 3s captures with --sample=cpu:200us I can actually spot eviction kernels, but they're interleaved with batching kernels. Any advice to make them stand out?

Lee: Two ideas: 1) Add more specific NVTX labels inside the eviction code (e.g., include batch id or phase) so you can filter/export by NVTX name later. 2) Temporarily reduce batch size or run a dev workload that triggers eviction-only flows — that makes traces much clearer.

Jess: Also check `nsys-ui` or `nsys stats --report=trace` and use the keyboard filtering to search NVTX names. You can export just the nvtx timeline which is tiny and inspect ordering without full cuda detail.

Sam: Great, thanks. Last question: any gotchas for capturing on Dedicated infra where other services run on the same box?

Lee: If you can't isolate the machine, use the `--target-pid` or `--target-process-name` filters, and prefer NVTX capture-range to avoid unrelated system activity. If the other services still contaminate traces, try enabling `--capture-backtrace` only for modules that matter (be mindful of overhead).

Jess: And remember to clean up leftover .nsys-rep files — they grow fast. Automate rotation with a short script that zips results after each run. :package:
